analogy.p: Imagine a rope pulled tight from the top of a tall pole down to a point on flat ground. The sun is directly overhead, so the pole's top casts a shadow of the rope on the ground: that shadow is the projection of the rope onto the plane. The angle between the rope and the ground is the angle between the rope and its shadow, and the pole, the shadow and the rope form a right-angled triangle that you can solve with SOHCAHTOA. The analogy breaks down because a real shadow depends on the direction of the light, whereas the projection in a maths problem always uses a light shining at exactly 90 degrees to the plane, straight down.
analogy.t: The shadow and the climbing rope

bullets: **3D Pythagoras**: the space diagonal of a cuboid with sides l, w, h is d = √(l² + w² + h²).
**3D trigonometry**: use sin, cos or tan in a right-angled triangle that lies **inside** a solid (often a vertical triangle).
**Angle between a line and a plane**: the angle between the line and its **projection** onto the plane.
You are expected to work with cuboids, prisms, pyramids, cones, and combinations of them.
You may also need the **sine and cosine rules** when the triangle in the solid is not right-angled.
Answers are normally to 3 significant figures for lengths and 1 decimal place for angles; keep full calculator accuracy in the middle of a calculation.
A neat, large, labelled **sketch of each flat triangle** you use earns method marks and prevents errors.
core.h: What the specification asks you to do
core.p: The Edexcel Higher specification expects you to apply **Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry in three dimensions**, including finding the angle between a line and a plane. In practice this means taking a solid such as a cuboid, prism or pyramid, spotting right-angled triangles hidden inside it, and solving them one after another. It is a problem-solving topic: the maths itself is only Pythagoras and SOHCAHTOA, but you must be able to see the triangles and sequence the steps. Questions are usually 4 to 6 marks on Paper 2 or Paper 3 and often end with 'work out the angle between ... and the plane ...'.

bullets: A **vertical edge** of a cuboid or prism is perpendicular to the base, so it forms a right angle with any line in the base that it touches.
The **diagonal of a face** is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle made from the two edges of that face.
A **space diagonal** joins opposite corners through the inside of the solid, and is the hypotenuse of a triangle with a face diagonal and an edge.
Mark right angles on your sketch; they tell you which triangles are right-angled.
The drawn angles in a 3D picture are **not** the true angles, so never measure from the drawing.
Label the true lengths on your flat triangle, not the apparent lengths on the 3D drawing.
Work out which lengths you need to find first, then plan the chain: (face diagonal) then (space diagonal) then (angle).
If you are given a net or plan view, use it: the plan shows true lengths in the horizontal base.
core.p: A 3D shape is just a collection of flat faces and cross-sections, and every right angle in the solid gives you a right-angled triangle. The skill is to pick out one flat triangle at a time and redraw it separately in 2D with its true side lengths. In a cuboid every edge meets the next at 90 degrees, so any vertical edge is perpendicular to the base and any horizontal line in the base. In a pyramid with its apex directly above the centre of the base, the vertical height is perpendicular to every line in the base through its foot. Redrawing triangles as flat diagrams removes the distortion of the perspective drawing and makes Pythagoras and trigonometry straightforward.

bullets: To find a **hypotenuse**: square both shorter sides, **add**, then square-root.
To find a **shorter side**: square the hypotenuse and the other side, **subtract** (hypotenuse² − side²), then square-root.
Example: a rectangle 12 cm by 5 cm has diagonal √(144 + 25) = √169 = 13 cm; this (5, 12, 13) triple is common in exams.
Other common triples: (3, 4, 5), (6, 8, 10), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25); spotting them saves calculator time.
Square-roots can be left as **surds** if the question asks for an exact answer, for example √185.
Check that your hypotenuse is longer than both other sides; if not, you have subtracted instead of added.
Units: keep the same units throughout, and write the answer in the units of length (cm, m).
A square of side s has diagonal s√2, which is useful in pyramid questions.
core.h: Pythagoras' theorem refresher and diagonals of faces
core.p: Pythagoras' theorem states that in a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: c² = a² + b². The hypotenuse is the longest side and is opposite the right angle. In 3D problems the first use is nearly always to find the diagonal of a rectangular face or of the base. For a rectangle of length l and width w, the diagonal x satisfies x² = l² + w², so x = √(l² + w²). This is the first step towards the space diagonal, and it is often the only step needed in the first part of a question.

bullets: Step 1: base diagonal x = √(l² + w²).
Step 2: space diagonal d = √(x² + h²) = √(l² + w² + h²).
Example: a cuboid 12 cm by 5 cm by 4 cm has x = 13 and d = √(169 + 16) = √185 = 13.6 cm (3 s.f.).
The space diagonal is always longer than any face diagonal and any edge.
There are exactly **four** space diagonals in a cuboid, all equal in length.
For a **cube** of side s, the space diagonal is s√3 (since d² = s² + s² + s² = 3s²).
Longest straight rod that fits in a box: the rod lies along the space diagonal, so it is the longest length that will fit inside a cuboid box.
To find a missing edge when d is known: h = √(d² − l² − w²).
core.h: The space diagonal of a cuboid
core.p: A cuboid has length l, width w and height h. The space diagonal d runs from one corner to the opposite corner through the middle of the solid. To find it, work in two steps: first find the diagonal x of the base using x² = l² + w², then form a vertical right-angled triangle with sides x and h and hypotenuse d, so d² = x² + h². Substituting gives **d² = l² + w² + h²**, so d = √(l² + w² + h²). This formula is Pythagoras applied twice, and it generalises 2D Pythagoras by one extra squared term. The two right angles you use are the right angle in the base, and the right angle between the vertical edge and the base.

bullets: **Projection** of a line onto a plane: the line joining the foot of the perpendicular from each point of the line to the plane.
The triangle used is: (point on the line) – (foot of the perpendicular on the plane) – (point where the line meets the plane).
The perpendicular is the **shortest** distance from the point to the plane and makes a right angle with every line in the plane through the foot.
If the angle between the line and plane is θ, then **sin θ = (perpendicular height) / (length of line)** and **tan θ = (perpendicular height) / (length of projection)**.
Never use the angle between the line and another **edge** of the solid unless the question asks for it; the angle with the plane is with the projection.
For a vertical line the angle with a horizontal plane is 90 degrees; for a horizontal line in the plane, the angle is 0 degrees.
The **angle of elevation** of a point above the ground is the angle between the line of sight and the horizontal plane through the observer, an everyday example of this definition.
core.h: Angle between a line and a plane - the key definition
core.p: The **angle between a line and a plane** is defined as the angle between the line and its **projection** onto the plane, where the projection is the 'shadow' of the line that you get by dropping perpendiculars from the line onto the plane. This is also the **smallest** angle that the line makes with any line in the plane. To find it you identify the foot of the perpendicular from a point on the line to the plane, which gives a right-angled triangle: the line is the hypotenuse, the perpendicular is the opposite side, and the projection is the adjacent side. The angle between the line and the plane is at the point where the line meets the plane.

bullets: Step 1: identify the **plane** (for example the base ABCD) and the **line** (for example AG).
Step 2: find the point on the plane directly below the top end of the line: G is above C, so the projection of AG is AC.
Step 3: sketch the right-angled triangle ACG with the right angle at C, and mark the angle GAC.
Step 4: find AC with Pythagoras (base diagonal), CG is the given height.
Step 5: use tan GAC = CG / AC (opposite over adjacent), then GAC = tan⁻¹(CG / AC).
Example: for the 12 by 5 by 4 cuboid, tan θ = 4 / 13, so θ = 17.1 degrees (1 d.p.).
Always state the triangle you use, for example 'In triangle ACG, angle ACG = 90 degrees'.
If you know the space diagonal, you could instead use sin θ = 4 / 13.6 = 0.294..., θ = 17.1 degrees; both routes agree.
core.h: Step-by-step method for finding the angle between a line and a plane
core.p: Follow the same procedure every time. First, name the line and the plane. Second, find the **projection** of the line onto the plane: this is the line joining the lower end of the line (where it meets the plane) to the point on the plane directly below the other end. Third, draw the right-angled triangle formed by the line, the perpendicular and the projection, redrawn flat. Fourth, work out the two sides you need (often with Pythagoras), choose sin, cos or tan, and use the inverse function. For a cuboid ABCDEFGH with the base ABCD, the angle between AG and the base is the angle GAC, because C is directly below G.

bullets: Half the base diagonal of a square of side s is **s√2 / 2**; for s = 10 this is 5√2 = 7.07 cm.
**Slant edge** VA: VA² = VO² + OA². For height 12 and side 10: VA² = 144 + 50 = 194, so VA = 13.9 cm (3 s.f.).
**Angle between a slant edge and the base**: angle VAO, with tan VAO = VO / OA = 12 / 7.07 = 1.697, so angle = 59.5 degrees.
**Slant height** of a face: √(height² + (s/2)²) = √(144 + 25) = 13 cm.
**Angle between a sloping face and the base**: angle at the base midpoint, tan = 12 / 5, so 67.4 degrees (a plane-plane angle, an extension).
The slant edges of a right square pyramid are all equal, so the four triangular faces are congruent.
The **volume** of a pyramid is ⅓ × base area × perpendicular height, which uses the vertical height (not the slant height).
If the apex is **not** above the centre (an oblique pyramid), find the foot of the perpendicular carefully from the given information.
core.h: Pyramids: height, slant edge and slant height
core.p: In a **right pyramid** the apex V is directly above the centre of the base. For a square base ABCD with centre O, the vertical height VO is perpendicular to the base, so triangle VOA is right-angled at O. The distance OA is **half the base diagonal**, which for a square of side s is s√2 / 2. The **slant edge** VA is the hypotenuse of triangle VOA. The **slant height** of a triangular face is the distance from the apex to the midpoint of a base edge, and it is the hypotenuse of a different right-angled triangle with the height and half the base side. Always check which of the two you need: edge or slant height.

bullets: Triangular prism: the rectangular faces are perpendicular to the triangular ends, so the edges along the length are perpendicular to the cross-section.
A line from one corner of the cross-section to the opposite far corner is the hypotenuse of a triangle formed by a cross-section side and the length.
Example cone: r = 6 cm, h = 8 cm gives slant height l = √(36 + 64) = 10 cm.
The semi-vertical angle of the cone with r = 6 and h = 8 is tan⁻¹(6 / 8) = 36.9 degrees (1 d.p.).
The **net** of a cone is a sector with radius l, so the curved surface area is πrl.
For a **sphere** there are no right-angled triangles to pick from the shape itself, but a plane section through the centre is a circle, so a chord-and-radius triangle is isosceles.
Frustums (cones with the top cut off) use similar triangles, linking to similarity and the scale factor topics.
Combined solids (a cylinder with a hemisphere on top) need the vertical heights adding up carefully.
core.p: A prism has a constant cross-section, so any 3D question on a prism reduces to the 2D cross-section plus a length. For a triangular prism with a right-angled triangle as its cross-section, you can use Pythagoras to find slanting edges and the diagonals of its rectangular faces. A wedge is a triangular prism lying on a rectangular face. Work out which vertical plane contains the line you want, then redraw it as a flat shape. For a **cone** with base radius r, vertical height h and slant height l, the triangle formed by h, r and l is right-angled at the centre of the base: l² = r² + h². The **semi-vertical angle** at the apex has tan = r / h.

bullets: Find the **line of intersection** of the two planes (for the pyramid it is a base edge).
At the midpoint of that line, draw one line in each plane perpendicular to the intersection; these two lines enclose the angle.
For the right square pyramid with base side 10 and height 12: the angle between a face and the base satisfies tan = 12 / 5, giving 67.4 degrees.
The triangle used has the **vertical height** as one side, and the distance from the centre to the midpoint of the base edge as the other (half the base side).
Check: the angle between a face and the base is larger than the angle between a slant edge and the base, because the face is steeper than the edge.
Do not confuse **slant height** (up a face, perpendicular to a base edge) with **slant edge** (along an edge to a corner).
In an exam the question usually says 'angle between plane X and plane Y' and the triangle is drawn on the diagram for you in part (a).
core.p: The angle between two planes that meet along a line is found by drawing, in each plane, a line that is **perpendicular to the line of intersection** at the same point. The angle between those two lines is the angle between the planes. In a right square pyramid, the angle between a triangular face and the base is found at the midpoint of a base edge: one line is along the base from the midpoint of the edge to the centre, the other is the slant height going up the face. In a cuboid, the angle between the plane ABGH (which slopes) and the base is found along edges perpendicular to the line AB. This is a harder Higher topic, but the technique is just the same: find the right-angled triangle that contains the angle.

bullets: Cosine rule for an angle: cos A = (b² + c² − a²) / (2bc), with all three sides found first.
Sine rule is useful for a side or angle when a pair is known: a / sin A = b / sin B.
Example: in a square pyramid, the angle between two adjacent slant edges at the apex is found by the cosine rule using two slant edges and the base side.
Area of a face triangle: ½ab sin C, where C is the angle at the apex between two slant edges.
First find every length by Pythagoras; then decide which rule from the data given (SAS or SSS).
Draw the 3D triangle as a separate flat diagram, labelling all three sides with their exact calculated lengths.
Surface area problems often combine 3D Pythagoras (slant height) with area of triangle formulae.
Always keep unrounded values (use ANS) until the final answer.
core.h: Using the sine and cosine rules inside solids
core.p: Not every triangle in a 3D solid is right-angled. If you are given the lengths of three sides of a triangle formed by three corners of the solid, you can find an angle with the **cosine rule**. If you are given an angle and two lengths in a non-right-angled triangle, you can use the **sine rule** or the cosine rule. You must first find the lengths of all the sides you need using Pythagoras, then apply the rule in a flat copy of the triangle. A typical question is to find the angle at A between the diagonals AC and AG, or the angle between two slant edges of a pyramid, or the angle subtended at the apex by an edge of the base.

bullets: Write √185 = 13.6014... before rounding to 13.6 cm.
Calculator in degree mode; check sin 30 = 0.5.
If a later part uses an earlier answer, use the **unrounded** value; examiners allow follow-through but accuracy is lost if you use a rounded value.
Inverse functions: tan⁻¹ (opposite / adjacent), sin⁻¹ (opposite / hypotenuse), cos⁻¹ (adjacent / hypotenuse).
An answer of 90 or more degrees for an angle with the base signals a mistake.
For 'show that' questions, work to one more figure than the target and state the final value.
core.p: A 3D question usually has several parts, and errors from rounding early can change the final answer. Keep full calculator values (use the memory or ANS) through the chain, and round only at the end to 3 significant figures for a length or 1 decimal place for an angle. If the question asks for an exact answer, leave the result as a surd, for example d = √185 or 5√2, and simplify surds where you can. Always include units, and check your answer is sensible: the space diagonal must be longer than every edge, an angle with the base must be less than 90 degrees, and a perpendicular height must be shorter than the hypotenuse.

bullets: Step 0: **find the triangle** - write 'Triangle ACG, right angle at C'.
Step 1: calculate the unknown side with Pythagoras (show the squares).
Step 2: choose SOH, CAH or TOA from the sides you know and write the ratio with numbers substituted.
Step 3: use the inverse function to find the angle, giving 1 decimal place unless stated.
Common 6-mark structure: find a face diagonal (2 marks), find the space diagonal or a slant edge (2 marks), find the angle (2 marks).
If the answer to an earlier part is given (for example 'AC = 13 cm'), use it even if you did not manage to show it.
Use correct vertex notation: angle GAC means the angle at A between AG and AC.
Do not lose marks for forgetting units: always write cm, m or degrees as appropriate.
core.p: 3D trigonometry rewards a calm, systematic approach. Read the question twice and underline what you must find. Draw a big sketch if one is not provided, or copy the given one and mark the right angles. Identify the line and plane in an angle question, then find the projection. Draw the triangle separately, label it and write down which trig ratio you use. Show every substitution because each correct step earns a method mark even when the final answer is wrong, and finish with the units. If you are stuck on a later part, try to use the given answer from an earlier part (these are often supplied).

bullets: **Plans and elevations**: the plan view shows true horizontal distances, which you can use as sides of the triangles.
**Bearings with elevation**: first find a horizontal distance using bearings and the cosine rule, then use tan for the height.
**Volume and surface area**: pyramid and cone problems often need a perpendicular height or slant height found by Pythagoras first.
**Vectors**: the magnitude of vector (a, b, c) in 3D is √(a² + b² + c²), the same as the space diagonal formula.
**Similarity**: sections of pyramids and cones parallel to the base are similar shapes; ratios of lengths are equal.
**Circle theorems**: a triangle inscribed in a semicircle has a right angle, which can create right-angled triangles in sections of a sphere or cone.
**Algebra**: you may need to rearrange d² = l² + w² + h² to find an unknown edge, or form an equation in x.
core.p: 3D trigonometry draws on many other topics. It is a direct application of Pythagoras and right-angled trigonometry, and uses the sine and cosine rules when triangles are not right-angled. It needs volume and surface area formulae, plans and elevations (viewing the solid from above, front and side), bearings and angles of elevation or depression (which combine horizontal bearings with vertical angles), and vectors (position vectors in 3D give the same lengths). Problems on towers and hills combine a bearing for horizontal direction with an angle of elevation for vertical rise.

exam: **Command words**: 'Calculate' or 'Work out' require method shown; 'Find the angle between the line AG and the plane ABCD' needs the projection identified; 'Give your answer to 3 significant figures' means round only at the end.
**2 mark** parts: one Pythagoras step, e.g. the base diagonal AC. M1 for the squares added, A1 for the length.
**3-4 mark** parts: two steps, e.g. a space diagonal. M1 for the base diagonal, M1 for the second Pythagoras, A1 for the answer.

**5-6 mark** questions: find lengths first, then the angle. Typical scheme: M1 find AC, M1 use triangle ACG, M1 trig ratio with numbers, M1 inverse function, A1 angle, with marks for correct use of the right triangle.
Write the triangle name and the right angle: 'In triangle ACG, angle ACG = 90°'. This signals the key idea to the examiner.
For 'angle between a line and a plane', write down which line is the projection: 'The projection of AG on the base is AC'.
Redraw triangles flat, with the true lengths; it takes ten seconds and prevents most errors.
If a length is given as a surd or exact value, keep it exact until the end.
Show the working for squares and square roots; it earns the method mark even with an arithmetic slip.
Check the answer is sensible: angle below 90 degrees, diagonal longer than every edge.
For 'show that' questions, start from the givens, show every step, and finish with the exact stated answer.

mistakes.r: d = √(l² + w² + h²); the base diagonal is only the first step.
mistakes.w: Using the space diagonal as √(l² + w²) (forgetting the height)

mistakes.r: Use the angle between the line and its projection on the plane, e.g. angle GAC, not angle GAB.
mistakes.w: Using the angle between the line and an edge instead of the plane

mistakes.r: The sketch is distorted; work out true lengths using calculation.
mistakes.w: Measuring angles or lengths on the 3D sketch

mistakes.r: Subtract to find a shorter side: a² = c² − b².
mistakes.w: Adding when finding a shorter side (using Pythagoras the wrong way round)

mistakes.r: Slant edge goes to a corner (use half the base diagonal); slant height goes to the midpoint of a base edge (use half the side).
mistakes.w: Confusing slant height with slant edge in pyramids

mistakes.r: The foot O is the centre; OA is half the diagonal, which is s√2 / 2 for a square.
mistakes.w: Using half the base side instead of half the base diagonal for the foot of the height to a corner

mistakes.r: Keep unrounded values (√185) or use ANS; round only the last answer.
mistakes.w: Rounding the intermediate value (e.g. 13.6) and getting the final angle slightly wrong

mistakes.r: Redraw the flat triangle, label opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to the angle, then choose SOH, CAH or TOA.
mistakes.w: Choosing the wrong trig ratio because the triangle was not redrawn

mistakes.r: An angle between a line and a plane lies between 0 and 90 degrees; check for errors.
mistakes.w: Giving an angle with the base greater than 90 degrees

summary: You must apply Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry to right-angled triangles hidden inside 3D solids such as cuboids, prisms, pyramids and cones, including finding space diagonals and the angle between a line and a plane. It is a multi-step problem-solving skill that mainly tests whether you can pick out and redraw the right triangle.

worked.q: ABCDEFGH is a cuboid. AB = 12 cm, BC = 5 cm and CG = 4 cm. (a) Calculate the length of AG. (b) Calculate the angle between AG and the base ABCD. (5 marks)
steps: Base diagonal: AC² = 12² + 5² = 144 + 25 = 169, so AC = 13 cm (M1, A1).
Triangle ACG has a right angle at C (CG is vertical). AG² = 13² + 4² = 169 + 16 = 185 (M1).
The projection of AG on the base is AC, so the angle is GAC. tan GAC = CG / AC = 4 / 13 (M1).

worked.q: A right pyramid has a square base ABCD of side 10 cm and vertical height 12 cm. The apex is V. Calculate (a) the length of the slant edge VA, (b) the angle between VA and the base. (5 marks)
steps: Triangle VOA is right-angled at O: VA² = 12² + 7.071...² = 144 + 50 = 194 (M1).
Angle VAO: tan VAO = VO / OA = 12 / 7.071... = 1.697 (M1).

worked.q: ABCDEFGH is a cuboid with AB = 8 cm, BC = 6 cm and CG = 5 cm. Calculate the size of angle GAB. (4 marks)
steps: Triangle ABG: AB is perpendicular to the face BCGF, so angle ABG = 90° (explain this).
BG is the diagonal of the rectangle BCGF: BG² = 6² + 5² = 61, so BG = √61 = 7.810... cm (M1, A1).
In right-angled triangle ABG, tan GAB = opposite / adjacent = BG / AB = 7.810... / 8 (M1).
